correctness.rationale: For any binary word the kth tortoise operation preserves prefix-count dominance: the transformed positions of each ordinal one are explicitly compared across words. This makes the phase-ordered output list monotone. At each rational phase cut, either total number of ones changes, or disjoint 01-to-10 swaps affect precisely one residue class. Equality under the kth iterate is equivalent to the last affected one being within the first k. Its rank is 1+floor(jp/q), yielding j<=H and excluding period multiples. Thus counting nonmultiples in the finite interval proves the formula and H not divisible q yields the sharp last collision. A packaged exact checker passes 49,750 parameter-iteration-length cases; finite checks corroborate, not replace, the proof.

originality.rationale: The full all-iteration rational-phase modular edge law (especially \(k\ge2\)), prefix-dominance mechanism, and sharp eventual-injectivity threshold do not follow from the previously established rational \(k=1\) count or the irrational all-k formula: at \(n\ge q\), the finite periodic language has only q factors, and every extra q-step crossing changes the collision residues. Campbell–Rampersad treats other sequences and proposes Sturmian variants; Carey–Clampitt studies different height-profile equivalence. No checked source states or logically dominates this all-k rational theorem. Earlier unindexed literature remains a residual priority risk.

value.rationale: Tortoise complexity is a recent, explicitly motivated way to quantify factor-image identifications. For the canonical rational Christoffel words the theorem settles every positive iterate and every length, exposes a modular oscillation when the factor language saturates at the period, proves a general binary order-preservation lemma, and determines a sharp all-k eventual-injectivity threshold. This is not a routine one-step parameter change or a finite-table computation.
